title: The Earth Laid Waste and the LORD Reigning on Zion
summary: The LORD lays waste the whole earth, and no class of people escapes: priest and people, master and slave, lender and borrower alike. The earth is defiled because its inhabitants have broken the everlasting covenant, so joy and wine vanish and the city of chaos falls. Songs of praise rise from the ends of the earth, but the prophet sees only treachery and a shaking world, until the LORD punishes the powers above and below and reigns in glory on Mount Zion.
story: Chapters 13 to 23 pronounced judgment on one nation after another: Babylon, Assyria, Philistia, Moab, Damascus, Egypt, Tyre. Chapter 24 lifts the camera from the map to the globe. The word for earth or land runs through the chapter again and again, and no nation is named at all. This opens the section of chapters 24 to 27, which gathers up the oracles against the nations into one picture of worldwide judgment followed by worldwide salvation. The chapter ends on the note the next three chapters will develop: the LORD will be king on Mount Zion. The feast of chapter 25, the songs of chapter 26, and the gathering of chapter 27 all flow from that final verse.
historical:
Chapters 24 to 27 are often called the Isaiah apocalypse, and when they were written is one of the long-running debates in the study of the book. The traditional view assigns them to Isaiah son of Amoz in the late eighth or early seventh century BC, noting that they follow naturally from the oracles against the nations and share vocabulary and themes with the rest of chapters 1 to 39. Some who hold an early date suggest that the fallen city in the background could be Babylon, which the Assyrian king Sennacherib destroyed in 689 BC. Many critical scholars have instead dated the section much later. Bernhard Duhm, writing at the end of the nineteenth century, placed it as late as the second century BC; most critical scholars since then have moved it earlier, to the late sixth, fifth, or fourth century BC, the Persian period after the exile, largely because of its universal scope, its themes of cosmic judgment and resurrection, and its likeness to later apocalyptic writing. The Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran, copied around the second century BC, already contains these chapters in their place, which makes the latest proposals difficult.

Part of the difficulty is that the chapter names no king, no empire, and no date. The unnamed city of verses 10 to 12 has been identified with Babylon, Nineveh, Samaria, Jerusalem, Tyre, Moab's capital, and others. Many readers now think the anonymity is deliberate: the city stands for every proud human city organized without God, and the section is meant to be read as a summing up rather than as a report on a single event.
cultural:
Verse 2 walks through the social order of an ancient town in pairs: priest and people, servant and master, maid and mistress, buyer and seller, lender and borrower. In ordinary life these distinctions decided who ate first, who owed whom, and who could be sold for debt. The judgment levels them all; rank protects no one. The collapse is described in the language of a harvest failure that every farming village understood: new wine drying up, vines withering, tambourines and harps falling silent. Wine and music marked the grape harvest and the festivals, so their disappearance is the sound of a community whose celebrations have stopped. The picture of an olive tree beaten and a vine gleaned (verse 13) comes from harvest practice, where after the main picking only a few fruits remained for the poor to glean. That is what is left of humanity.

The phrase "the windows of heaven are open" (verse 18) would have reminded any Israelite of the flood (Genesis 7:11), and the "everlasting covenant" of verse 5 recalls the covenant God made with Noah and every living creature (Genesis 9:16). Ancient peoples also believed that the sun, moon, and stars were powers or gods. Verse 21's "host of heaven" can mean the stars themselves or the spiritual powers people worshiped through them, and verse 23 pictures the sun and moon ashamed before the true King.
literary: The chapter is poetry built on repetition and sound. Hebrew wordplay runs through it: verse 3 doubles its verbs to intensify them ("utterly laid waste and thoroughly plundered"), and verse 17 strings together three similar-sounding words for terror, pit, and snare (pachad, pachat, pach), so that the reader hears the trap closing. The structure moves in waves. Verses 1 to 3 announce the judgment; verses 4 to 13 explain it and describe the dead city; verses 14 to 16a let songs of praise break in from the far west and the coastlands; verse 16b interrupts with the prophet's own grief; verses 17 to 20 return to the shaking earth; and verses 21 to 23 end with the LORD reigning. The swing between lament and praise is characteristic of chapters 24 to 27. Scholars often call these chapters proto-apocalyptic: they share the cosmic scale and end-of-the-age horizon of later apocalypses such as Daniel, but lack their visions, angelic interpreters, and coded beasts.

outline.t: The LORD lays waste the earth, sparing no class
The earth defiled by a broken covenant
Joy silenced and the city of chaos shattered
Songs from the ends of the earth and the prophet's grief
Terror, pit, and snare: the earth staggers
The powers punished and the LORD reigning on Zion

doctrines.note: The judgment is universal because the guilt is universal: the earth is "defiled by its people" (verse 5). No status exempts anyone, and even the powers of heaven are held to account. Judgment here is the moral order of creation giving way under human rebellion.

Humanity as a whole is said to have broken "the everlasting covenant." Many interpreters connect this with God's covenant with Noah and all creation, which would mean that even nations without the law of Moses stand accountable to their Creator.
The chapter ends with the LORD of Hosts reigning on Mount Zion before his elders with great glory. The destruction is not the last word; it clears the ground for God's open kingship over the world.

words.note: Erets, earth or land. The word appears sixteen times in this chapter. It can mean a single country or the whole world, and the ambiguity is part of the chapter's force: what happens to one land becomes a picture of what happens to all. Most translations render it earth here because of the universal scope of verses 1 to 6 and 17 to 23.

Berit, covenant. A binding relationship sealed by oath, with obligations and consequences. Here it is called everlasting (verse 5), a phrase used of God's covenant with Noah, with Abraham, and with David. Its breach explains why the earth itself falls under a curse.

Bagad, to act treacherously. Verse 16 repeats the root five times in a single line, a deliberate pileup that the BSB renders "The treacherous betray; the treacherous deal in treachery." The word describes faithlessness inside a relationship, the betrayal of a spouse or an ally, and it explains why the prophet cannot yet join the songs of praise.

christ: The chapter's end, the LORD reigning on Zion in glory, is the hope the Gospels announce as the kingdom of God drawing near in Jesus. The link to Christ here is thematic rather than a direct prediction: the chapter describes the whole earth under judgment and God's rule established over it, and the New Testament places that final judgment and reign in the hands of the risen Christ (Acts 17:31). Revelation borrows this chapter's imagery, the shaken earth, the powers punished and bound, and a city where sun and moon are no longer needed because God's glory is its light (Revelation 21:23). The New Testament also insists that the one who judges is the one who bore judgment, which is why the prophet's cry of grief in verse 16 is not the church's final word.

hard.q: Is it just for God to lay waste the whole earth, including people who never heard of Israel's covenant?
hard.a:
The chapter itself raises the question by making the judgment universal. Its answer is that all humanity stands in a covenant relationship with God as Creator: the earth is defiled because its people "have transgressed the laws" and broken the everlasting covenant, which many interpreters read as the covenant with Noah that bound all people to honor life (Genesis 9). Paul makes a similar argument in Romans 1 and 2, that people without the written law still know enough of God and of right and wrong to be accountable.

Two other features of the chapter matter. It is poetry of vision, gathering all human rebellion into one picture, and readers differ over how much it describes a single final event and how much it describes the pattern of every judgment in history. And the chapter does not delight in the destruction: the prophet cries out that he is wasting away. Judgment in Isaiah is always followed by the offer of a feast for all peoples, which comes in the very next chapter.

questions: Verse 2 says the judgment falls on priest and people, master and servant alike. What false securities, of status, money, or religion, does this chapter strip away?
The prophet hears songs of praise but cannot join them because he sees the treachery around him (verse 16). When is grief a more honest response than celebration?
The chapter ends with the LORD reigning on Zion. How does knowing the end of the story change the way someone lives through a time when the world seems to be coming apart?
